lesson.title: Hidden Twins: Body & Home
lesson.subtitle: arm, hand, vinger, hoofd, oog, oor — the body is the safest place to start

hook.title: Your Body Already Speaks Dutch
hook.content: The body is where English and Dutch look most alike. Arm is arm, hand is hand, vinger is finger, and oor is ear. These are not lucky borrowings; they are the oldest layer of the family.

pattern.title: Six twins, two articles
pattern.content: De arm, de hand, de vinger are common-gender words; het hoofd, het oog and het oor are neuter. You do not have to guess yet — read the article as part of the word, the way English reads 'the' as part of a phrase.
pattern.trap_note: Vinger starts with v, but the English twin starts with f. Dutch voices the old f in spelling even when a northern speaker says it close to f.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Hidden Twins: Body & Home):
exercises.target_answer: de arm, de hand, de vinger, het hoofd, het oog, het oor
exercises.meaning: arm, hand, finger, head, eye, ear
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Hidden Twins: Body & Home": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “My hand is warm.”?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn hand is warm.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Hidden Twins: Body & Home”.

cues: The pattern: Six twins, two articles
It means: My head is cold.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn hoofd is koud.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Six twins, two articles.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Vinger starts with v, but the English twin starts with f. Dutch voices the old f in spelling even when a northern speaker says it close to f.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn oog is open.” is word-for-word “My eye is open.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Six twins, two articles.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: My ear is small.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn oor is klein.” reuses only material taught in “Hidden Twins: Body & Home” — Six twins, two articles.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Mijn oor is klein.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Six twins, two articles.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “My finger is small.”
twist.explanation: Vinger is the f→v twin of finger, and the sentence reuses the same possessive frame.

payoff.text: The direct-twin principle from the opening lesson now carries a whole semantic field.

summary.outcome: Name six body parts with their articles and use mijn before a noun.
summary.takeaway: The body vocabulary is nearly free; the only new work is the article that travels with each noun.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: The SCH Bridge.

arm.etymology_derivation: The same body word as English arm.

hand.etymology_derivation: The same body word as English hand.

vinger.etymology_derivation: English finger and Dutch vinger are the same word; f voiced to v.

hoofd.etymology_derivation: English head and Dutch hoofd are cognate; both lost sounds in different places.

oog.etymology_derivation: English eye and Dutch oog are the same body word.

oor.etymology_derivation: English ear and Dutch oor are the same body word.
